Kyiv residents rescued as Russian strikes damage buildings across the city Copy/paste the link below: Copy Copy/paste the article video embed link below: Copy Updated: 20/08/2026 - 10:16 GMT+2 Russia’s overnight missile barrage killed at least 12 people in Kyiv on Thursday, 20 August, as residents were rescued from damaged buildings and firefighters battled fires across the capital. … More At least 33 people were wounded, according to Ukraine’s Emergency Service, while the air-raid alert remained in force into the early hours. ADVERTISEMENT ADVERTISEMENT The strikes hit 12 locations in the Darnytskyi, Sviatoshynskyi and Solomianskyi districts, damaging residential buildings, a medical facility and an educational institution. Fires broke out at warehouses, vehicles and other non-residential sites, adding to the pressure on emergency crews working across the city. The top two floors of a nine-storey apartment block in Solomianskyi district were destroyed, with fires raging on several floors. Rescuers pulled nine injured people from the rubble, but two residents were killed. Nearby homes, a children’s hospital and vehicles were also damaged. The overnight barrage came as Russia stepped up its use of ballistic missiles against Kyiv, placing further strain on Ukraine’s air-defence network. Kyiv has only a limited number of systems capable of intercepting ballistic threats, while supplies of interceptor missiles for US-made Patriot batteries remain constrained. Electricity was also cut to about 90,000 homes after the attack, although the power company DTEK said more than half had been reconnected. https://www.gazettelive.co.uk/news/teess.text: A Teessider accused of murdering his student stepdaughter amid a "dangerous sexual obsession" did not tell anyone he had visited her in the hours before she died, a jury has heard. Hartlepool man Nathan Owens is on trial at Preston Crown Court in Preston accused of murdering 19-year-old Carla Georgescu, who was found dead at her university halls of residence. The 35-year-old defendant denies the charge, as well as charges of strangulation and grievous bodily harm (GBH). It is alleged Owens attacked Carla with a knife and strangled her before discarding her phone, laptop, bedding and sexual items in the countryside as he returned home before dawn. Prosecutors allege it was the culmination of a 'dangerous sexual obsession' with Carla, reports Lancs Live. Jurors have been told how Owens was the last person to see Carla alive after driving from Hartlepool to Preston in the early hours of February 4, 2025. The prosecution alleges that in the days before Carla died Owens accessed videos of himself having sex with an effigy wearing Carla's nightdress and with her toy dolls. The court heard that when detectives examined her bedroom they discovered Owens' DNA on her body and in the room and a sex toy close to her body. On the second day of the trial, today - Wednesday, October 7 - the jury heard how Owens' wife - Carla's mother - was completely unaware of the early-hours visit while she was asleep at their home in Hopps Street, Hartlepool. Janina Georgescu told the court she only learned her husband had left the house the day after her daughter had been discovered dead. Speaking from the witness box, she described how her daughter was 'happy and excited' when she had visited her on the weekend of January 31. She said they had shopped for birthday gifts and spent the evening at Carla's accommodation - Ribble Hall - before Owens joined them for dinner the following day. Ms Georgescu told the jury: "I would say she was excited and very happy. Perhaps the most happy I have seen her since she was a child. Things were going really well for her." She told the court how Carla was looking forward to taking her best friend to a concert in Romania and meeting up with her online boyfriend for the first time. She said she had also written a book and was speaking to agents about getting it published. Ms Georgescu said that on February 5 she became worried that her daughter was not picking up her messages and told the jury how she had asked campus security to check on her. A few hours later, Ms Georgescu, a clinical psychiatrist, said she received a telephone call from the police saying they would be visiting her at home. She added: "I was on the couch and I said, 'the police are coming.' Of course I knew what that meant because I had the same experience when Carla's father passed away. "I think he [Mr Owens] appeared sad. I'm not very sure because I was in a state and I was not very perceptive but I think his eyes welled up and he turned red. He didn't say anything. "He got up and I knew he was coming towards me to comfort me and I said, 'don't come near me', so he went to the kitchen area to start tidying things up." She said when officers told them Carla had died - and it appeared she had taken her own life - her husband began to cry. Ms Georgescu said she said she was 'shocked and very angry' when the police left, adding: "I don't remember what he [Owens] said to me. I remember he was crying. I went over and hugged him. I wasn't crying." She said Owens then offered to make the funeral arrangements - but still did not mention he had seen Carla in the early hours of February 4. She said it was only when she spoke to the mortuary the following day that the defendant admitted he had been in Preston. Ms Georgescu said Owens claimed Carla had asked him to help clear some rubbish from her bedroom and take some incontinence pants to her, and he had agreed. She said that on February 4, Owens had been 'his normal self' and they had been shopping together and taken a walk on the beach near their home. At this time it is alleged Carla was lifeless in her bedroom at Ribble Hall, Preston, and had not yet been discovered. Ms Georgescu also told jurors how Carla and Owens had a good relationship and Carla was 'tactile' with her stepfather. She said that when her husband said he had been to help her daughter in the night she believed it was the sort of thing he would do. The court heard a statement from Carla's online boyfriend, who said they had met through shared interests in Instagram in 2025. From November they considered themselves a couple and they planned to meet up in Romania in February 2026. They messaged every day and spoke once on the phone, shortly before Christmas 2025, he said. In a statement to the police in Romania, where he lives, he said they had discussed sexual fantasies but from what Carla had told him he believed she was a virgin. He said they last chatted on Instagram's messaging around three hours before it is alleged Carla was murdered. Mr Botzja messaged Carla to say goodnight, as they did every night, telling her: "I feel like I'm falling in love again. We will see how things go in the real world... love ya xxx" The jury was told how Carla replied: "Goodnight beautiful". Carla's was described by university friends as kind and positive and was planning for her future as a child psychologist. She had discussed returning to Romania after her studies and told friends she had never wanted to move to England with her mother as a child. In January 2025 she had asked a member of the university's Neurodiversity Society for dating advice, saying she had 'internalised purity culture' and 'needed her first time to be special.' A student counsellor, who saw her five times before she died, described Carla as 'childlike' and 'not as worldly' as other students her age. However he said although she was naive, Carla was intelligent, articulate and philosophical. He said Carla had disclosed 'fleeting' suicidal thoughts but he had no concerns she would act on them and was satisfied she could keep herself safe. Mr Owens, of Hopps Street, Hartlepool, denies murder; strangulation; and GBH. The trial continues. https://www.theguardian.com/business/202.text: Vessels at the strait of Hormuz, as seen from Musandam, Oman. Photograph: Reuters View image in fullscreen Vessels at the strait of Hormuz, as seen from Musandam, Oman. Photograph: Reuters Oil Oil prices jump to five-month high as attacks threaten global supply Iran’s IRGC says it hit four vessels in the northern Gulf and three more struck mines near the strait of Hormuz Shipping workers: how is the Middle East conflict affecting you? Lauren Almeida Thu 22 Oct 2026 07.28 EDT Last modified on Thu 22 Oct 2026 12.10 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google Oil prices jumped to a five-month high on Thursday after ​attacks in Saudi Arabia and hits to tankers in the strait of Hormuz threatened further disruptions to the world’s crude supply. Brent crude, the international benchmark for oil prices, rose by 3% to hit $112 a barrel for first time since 18 May. Yemeni Houthis , who are aligned with Iran, hit several targets in Saudi Arabia on Wednesday, with two people killed and eight more wounded in a civilian airport in Dammam, and two people killed in a drone attack on a Saudi oilfield. Elsewhere the Iranian Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) said four vessels involved in “illegal” oil transfers in the northern ​Gulf were hit and caught fire after being tracked by its forces on Wednesday. It said three more vessels collided with mines west of the strait of Hormuz, and warned the US that continued provocations could lead to a wider response against its regional bases. A chart showing the Brent crude oil price The US has now ordered some diplomats and family members to leave their missions in Saudi Arabia, and it plans to withdraw family members from a number of other missions in the Middle East, according to Reuters, which also reported that Saudi Aramco has instructed staff to evacuate its headquarters in Dhahran and work remotely. Concern is growing that conflict in the region could escalate further, almost eight months after Tehran’s effective block on the strait of Hormuz triggered what many feared would bring the greatest energy supply disruption in the history of the market. In the first weeks after the US-Israeli attacks on Iran , oil surged past $100 a barrel and market observers predicted prices of up to $150 a barrel as flows through Hormuz came to a halt. Oil peaked at $126 a barrel in April during the conflict and fell back below $100 in late May and then to lows of $71 at the start of July amid hopes of a ceasefire in the region. The price began to climb again after the memorandum of understanding between the US and Iran fell apart and fresh hostilities broke out in the Gulf . However, data from Kpler has shown that oil exports from the Persian Gulf have now risen above their prewar levels, partly because of an increase in oil pumped overland through pipelines to the Red Sea and Gulf of Oman. Global stocks wobbled on Thursday amid expectations of higher inflation and borrowing costs. The Stoxx Europe 600, which tracks the biggest companies on the continent, fell by 1%, with the UK’s FTSE 100 down by 0.7%. skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Every weekday Sign up to Business Today Get set for the working day – we'll point you to all the business news and analysis you need every morning after newsletter promotion In Asia, Japan’s Nikkei 225 index dropped 2.7%, while the South Korean Kospi fell 3.5%. Hong Kong’s Hang Seng index shed 3%. Shares in American Airlines dropped almost 4% in pre-market trading after the company warned that high fuel costs would push it into a loss this year. American Airlines abandoned its previous forecast that it might achieve a profit this year as it faced “historic fuel cost pressure”. https://www.politico.eu/article/meet-the.text: FRANKFURT — The race to replace Christine Lagarde has reached fever pitch after she officially announced her intention to depart the European Central Bank in February next year. The two leading contenders are familiar figures from the eurozone’s central banking circuit: Spain’s Pablo Hernández de Cos, a measured economist with a reputation for quiet authority, and Dutchman Klaas Knot, a former hawk whose years on the ECB’s governing council left a more complicated legacy. A recent Bloomberg survey of economists gives de Cos a slender lead: 12 respondents picked him, against nine for Knot. The survey offers a snapshot of expert preferences, not a forecast of the outcome. EU leaders will make the appointment, with national claims and other ECB vacancies likely to shape negotiations. Advertisement Advertisement The choices will also be influenced by horse trading over what will likely be a package deal with the opportunity to fill the two executive board seats that will be vacant in January and May. Softly spoken de Cos An economist with a Ph.D. from the University of Madrid, de Cos joined the Bank of Spain in 1997, moved to Frankfurt in 2004 to be an adviser to the ECB’s executive board, before returning to the Spanish central bank. He rose through the ranks to become governor, serving from 2018 to 2024. In this role he restored the Bank of Spain’s reputation after a series of missteps before and during the financial crisis. His achievement was implicitly acknowledged by his appointment to two terms as chair of the Basel Committee for Banking Supervision, the global standard-setter for bank regulation. He now runs the Bank for International Settlements, the institution often described as the central bankers’ central bank. His style is low-key: a modest dove, meaning that he is more attentive than hawks to growth and employment alongside inflation. Still, when inflation surged in 2022, de Cos backed the ECB’s shift toward higher rates. Equally, he has little time for governments that put off essential pension system reforms, having published a sharp critique of the Pedro Sanchez government while at the Bank of Spain. His case De Cos has long been groomed by Lagarde’s predecessor Mario Draghi, whose voice continues to carry a heavy weight in European economic debates and may influence the preference of some countries as they mull who to place at the top of the Frankfurt institution. As France faces mounting debt pressures, de Cos’ experience as a senior Bank of Spain economist during the eurozone crisis could convince EU governments that he is the best fit. Galo Nuño, vice dean and professor of economics at IE University and a former alternate member of the ECB governing council, called it “a huge advantage.” Advertisement Advertisement His challenges The political arithmetic, however, could work against the Spaniard. France is keen to secure the role of the ECB chief economist, which becomes vacant in May 2027. Some officials may want to avoid pairing the ECB presidency and chief economist roles with candidates from highly indebted countries. With inflation above target and the eurozone having lived through a severe inflation shock in 2022, some leaders may prefer a candidate with a more clearly hawkish record. Enter: Klaas Knot. Knot: hawk turned pragmatist Knot also has a strong economic background, boasting a Ph.D. from the University of Groningen. After early positions at the Dutch central bank, De Nederlandsche Bank, and the International Monetary Fund, he moved into senior roles at the Dutch Finance Ministry and returned to the DNB, which he led from 2011 to 2025. He has also chaired the Financial Stability Board, the global body tasked with monitoring risks to the financial system. For much of Draghi’s presidency, Knot was a staunch hawk who publicly challenged the ECB’s stimulus measures. In September 2019, he called the package “disproportionate.” His relationship with the ECB’s leadership was more harmonious under Lagarde. He supported both her pandemic crisis response package, PEPP, as well as the Transmission Protection Mechanism — a potentially more radical tool than any brought in under Draghi which allows the ECB to buy up unlimited debt of a single EU member country. Advertisement Advertisement Knot remained an early advocate of raising rates when inflation took off but came to be described as a pragmatic hawk and team player. His case Supporters argue that a hawkish president could help the ECB support Southern European economies during a debt crisis while reassuring consumers and investors that the bank remains committed to price stability. Knot’s former role as chair of the G20’s Financial Stability Board could also boost his case. Berenberg chief economist Holger Schmieding argued that “the question who may be best placed to deal with potential financial turbulences will likely play a key role in the choice of new ECB leaders.” This role was also Draghi’s springboard. His challenges Germany’s ambitions could be a stumbling block, as Northern European hawks will have had their turn with Knot. EFG Bank chief economist Stefan Gerlach said: “If Knot is appointed, then Germany can hardly argue that it is its turn to appoint the president after him.” Some veteran governors still view Knot’s public break with Draghi as disloyal. What happens now? German Chancellor Friedrich Merz said a decision would be taken by year-end, with eurozone ministers set to gather under the banner of the European Council in mid-December. Advertisement Advertisement When it comes who will win the race, the history could cut both ways. Nuño, who has seen both candidates in action, said each brings monetary-policy expertise and the political pragmatism needed to manage the challenges ahead. The choice, then, will turn on which mix of policy temperament and political arithmetic EU leaders want at the top.

https://www.prokerala.com/news/articles/.text: Bucharest, Oct 17 : All nine Indian seafarers on board chemical tanker YARA J are safe and the vessel has arrived at the Port of Constanta in Romania, the Embassy of India in Bucharest said on Saturday. The confirmation came after India's Ambassador to Romania, Manoj Mohapatra, spoke with Romanian authorities and the Company Security Officer (CSO) of the tanker. "Amb. Manoj Mohapatra spoke with Romanian authorities, including SAR Romania and MRCC Constanta, as well as the CSO of the chemical tanker YARA J (IMO: 9221803). It was confirmed that all nine Indian seafarers on board are safe and the vessel has arrived at the Port of Constanta. The Ambassador assured them of the Government of India's full support and assistance," the Embassy posted on X. Last week, three Indian nationals rescued from the commercial vessel MV Royad Mammadov, which came under attack in the Black Sea, departed from Romania for India, the Embassy had said. "Three Indian nationals, Shri Sahil Sandhu, Shri Ashwini Kumar and Shri Harman Singh, departed for India today. The Embassy provided all necessary support and assistance to facilitate their return," the Embassy had posted on X. "We express our sincere gratitude to the Romanian authorities, Constanta County Hospital, and the Romanian rescue teams for their invaluable assistance, cooperation and support," it added. The three Indians were rescued from the vessel on October 6. On October 7, India condemned attacks targeting commercial vessels in the Black Sea region and reiterated its call for dialogue and diplomacy to de-escalate tensions and enable an early return of peace in the region. Addressing a bi-weekly media briefing in New Delhi, Ministry of External Affairs (MEA) spokesperson Randhir Jaiswal said that attacks targeting commercial vessels threaten commercial shipping and endanger the lives of the seafaring community. "We have seen a string of attacks targeting commercial vessels in the Black Sea region in the last one or two days. We condemn such attacks that threaten commercial shipping and endanger lives of our seafaring community. First, the commercial vessel MV Royad Mammadov came under attack while it was flying in the Black Sea. There were three Indian nationals onboard. All of them are safe, but one of them got injured, and he is receiving treatment. We thank the Romanian authorities who lent us a helping hand and have been very helpful in this particular incident," Jaiswal added. https://www.politico.eu/article/merz-cla.text: BERLIN — German Chancellor Friedrich Merz on Tuesday reiterated his push to link the EU’s next budget to unanimous backing for a multibillion-euro Ukraine loan, despite Slovak Prime Minister Robert Fico labeling the demand “classic blackmail.” Supporting Ukraine “is a shared European responsibility, not the responsibility of individual member states,” Merz told reporters at a press conference with Hungarian Prime Minister Péter Magyar. “That is why the question of how we will finance Ukraine in the coming years, if necessary, naturally belongs within the context of these budget negotiations.” Merz’s demand, which he also laid out in a letter to European Council President António Costa on Friday, has triggered a backlash. “What the German chancellor is doing is classic blackmail, and I reject it,” Fico said Tuesday during a meeting with Czech Prime Minister Andrej Babiš in Bratislava, according to Slovak media . Advertisement Advertisement The EU and partners are currently discussing a new €70 billion loan to support Ukraine in the next year against sustained Russian attacks. The EU plans to shoulder about €45 billion of the loan, while other allies like Britain, Canada and Japan are expected to stump up the remaining €25 billion. Merz argued that he does not want to repeat last year’s approach, when a different €90 billion loan for Ukraine was agreed only with financial guarantees and liabilities from most EU countries, while three nations — Czechia, Hungary and Slovakia — secured an opt-out. “In my view, continuing down this path is not a good option. We must fully incorporate Ukraine policy into the EU budget,” he said. However, that view is not shared by Magyar, who came to Berlin with four ministers and a state secretary to discuss deeper cooperation, underlining the general rapprochement between Germany and Hungary after years of icy relations under Budapest’s previous leader Viktor Orbán. “I would like to note here — diplomatically and with all due respect as the Hungarian prime minister — that I do not necessarily consider it the right approach for the European budget, which is actually intended for seven years and for Europe,” to be “linked to other matters,” Magyar said.
